1.pericope_label: Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon
debates: Why the city is called a virgin
Whether the oracle is a warning or a sentence already passed
Whether the chapter speaks of literal Babylon only or of a later antitype
outliers: Calvin denies the moral sense of virgin that the word would naturally carry, referring it only to a city never yet forced
themes: A command issued as though from the judgment-seat
Luxury named as the ground of the reversal
The captor made to do the captive work
An empire treated as a woman stripped of rank

3.pericope_label: Thy nakedness uncovered; sit thou silent
debates: How the clause I will not meet thee as a man should be rendered
Whether the verse about the Redeemer is original or an intrusion into the text
Whether the silence commanded marks shame or subjection
outliers: Ellicott raises the possibility that the Redeemer verse began as a marginal note, a suggestion none of the others entertain
themes: Prosperity as a veil over old crimes
A judgment that admits no intercession
A song of praise breaking into an oracle of doom
Loudness answered by enforced silence

6.pericope_label: I shall be a lady for ever; I am, and none else beside me
debates: Whether an instrument of judgment is guilty for executing it
What the boast I am and none else beside me claims
Whether two verses here belong to the original text
outliers: Clarke reports one of his oldest manuscripts as lacking both the sixth and seventh verses, a textual doubt none of the others raise
themes: A commission exceeded by the one who held it
Reverence for age as the measure of cruelty
Prosperity mistaken for exemption from the common lot
A creature borrowing the language of the Creator

9.pericope_label: Two things in one day: loss of children and widowhood
debates: Which siege of Babylon fulfilled the prophecy
Whether the phrase means in their completeness or suddenly
Whether the sorceries are a cause of the ruin or something powerless to prevent it
outliers: Clarke sets aside the received reading in favour of one attested only by two ancient translations
themes: Boasted security answered by simultaneous loss
Empire described as robbery on a large scale
Wickedness renamed to make it presentable
A conscience silenced by refusing to look

11.pericope_label: Stand now with thine enchantments; let the astrologers save thee
debates: Whether a phrase has dropped out of the eleventh verse
Whether the challenge means come near or persevere
What the three titles for the astrologers denote
outliers: Clarke argues a phrase is lost from the text although no ancient version preserves a trace of it, and declines to conjecture a replacement
themes: A calamity that cannot be foreseen or charmed away
Irony as the form the sentence takes
Counsel multiplied into weariness
Sky-watching answered by a fire that leaves no coal

14.pericope_label: As stubble the fire shall burn; none shall save thee
debates: Whether the merchants are literal traders, allies, or the diviners under a contemptuous name
Whether the final verse should be read as one statement or two
What the last phrase of the chapter means
outliers: Wesley rearranges the clauses of the final verse to make sorcerers and merchants two separate subjects, where the others read one
themes: Stubble chosen over wood as the image of uselessness
Astrology as a way of emptying providence of God
A fire that gives no warmth
Every helper departing on his own road
